title: Months of daytime sleepiness in a 48-year-old scientist
desc: This station is a focused fatigue and sleep history, with a targeted examination, of Martha, a 48-year-old scientist seeing her GP. For several months she has felt sleepy and unrefreshed, and she is making errors at work. She snores heavily, drinks wine before bed and smokes, and she has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her sleep screening questionnaires and blood results. They should diagnose probable obstructive sleep apnoea, exclude the main differentials, arrange a sleep study, give driving advice and lifestyle measures, outline the treatment options and safety-net.
focus: Fatigue: telling sleepiness from fatigue, screening the differentials with cluster questions and a sleep history, then recognising and working up obstructive sleep apnoea in general practice
stem: You are the junior doctor working in a general practice. Martha is a 48-year-old scientist who has come in because she has been feeling very tired. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first and is available in the next room.
tasks: Take a focused history from Martha and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you her sleep screening questionnaire results and her blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Martha, a 48-year-old scientist (date of birth 9 June 1978). You look tired and yawn a few times during the consultation. You are friendly but a little flat, and frustrated that you can't seem to shake this. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "Hi doctor, I've just been feeling so awfully tired lately! It has been getting worse and worse."

The tiredness (give only when asked):

  • Onset: several months. You can't remember exactly when it started. It has crept up gradually and is getting worse.
  • Timing: you are tired throughout the day.
  • What it feels like: only if the candidate asks whether it is sleepiness or lack of energy, or whether you fall asleep: "It's more that I'm sleepy. I feel like I could nod off any time I sit still."
  • Severity: 8 out of 10.
  • Worse: "It's worse when I have a long day of work, I just can't stay awake!"
  • Cause: you are unsure what is causing it.
  • Impact: you are making a lot of errors at work, and your concentration and memory are poor. You have no energy to exercise.
  • Mood: lately you have been feeling a bit down, and you put it down to being so sleepy. You still enjoy things when you have the energy. No thoughts of self-harm or suicide (only if asked).

Sleep (give only when asked):

  • You go to bed at about 11 pm and sleep about 7 hours.
  • You wake up feeling poorly rested and unrefreshed, "like I haven't slept at all".
  • You wake during the night and aren't sure why, but you fall back asleep easily.
  • Snoring: your partner tells you that you are a chronic, heavy snorer. Your partner is a heavy sleeper, so has never said whether you stop breathing or gasp in your sleep.
  • Alcohol: you have a glass or two of wine before bed most nights: "I think it helps me have a better sleep."
  • If asked: you have 2 or 3 coffees a day, none after lunch. You sometimes have a dry mouth in the morning. No morning headaches. No sleeping tablets.

Driving (only if asked specifically): you drive about 25 minutes each way to work. After long days you sometimes feel drowsy on the drive home and wind the window down to stay awake. No crashes or near misses.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all absent):

  • Thyroid: no feeling cold, no constipation, no dry skin or hair changes. Your weight has crept up a few kilos over the last couple of years.
  • Menopause: your periods are still regular and normal. No hot flushes or night sweats. You are not menopausal yet.
  • Anaemia: periods not heavy, no blood in the stool or black stools, no breathlessness or palpitations.
  • Cancer: no weight loss, no night sweats, no fevers, no lumps, no bleeding.
  • Heart and lungs: no breathlessness, no chest pain, no need to sleep propped up, no waking breathless, no ankle swelling. No long-standing cough, phlegm or wheeze.
  • Diabetes: no excessive thirst or passing lots of urine, no hypos.

Past medical history: high blood pressure for 5 years. Type 2 diabetes for 10 years. Not menopausal yet.

Medications: perindopril 5 mg daily and metformin 500 mg daily. No over-the-counter medicines, supplements or sleeping tablets. Allergies: none known.

Family history: your parents are alive and well. No siblings.

Social history:

  • Smoking: 10 cigarettes a day for 20 years.
  • Alcohol: a glass or two of wine before bed most nights.
  • Diet: "Could be better."
  • Exercise: none; you have no energy for it.
  • Work: a laboratory scientist. You are not doing well at work at the moment because of the mistakes.
  • You live with your partner.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are unsure what is causing this. You hope it is not something bad. You would like to find out what is wrong and get back to feeling normal.

Question to raise (near the end if the candidate has not asked about your worries): "It's not something bad, is it, doctor?"

If asked something outside the script, give a realistic answer consistent with the story.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: alert, yawning, centrally obese woman. Not pale, not cyanosed, not short of breath. Affect slightly flat.
  • Vital signs: HR 82 beats/min regular; BP 148/92 mmHg; RR 16/min; SpO2 96% on room air; temperature 36.6 °C.
  • Measurements: weight 98 kg, height 165 cm (BMI 36.0). Waist circumference 112 cm. Neck circumference 42 cm.
  • Hands: mild nicotine staining of the right fingers. No clubbing, no pallor of the palmar creases, no tremor.
  • Face and eyes: no conjunctival pallor. Jaw normal in size and position (no retrognathia).
  • Nose: both nostrils patent; no polyps.
  • Oropharynx: Crowded. Large tongue; with the mouth open and tongue out only the soft palate and base of the uvula are visible (Mallampati class III). Low-lying soft palate, long uvula; tonsils small (grade 1).
  • Neck: no goitre, no lymphadenopathy.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds dual, no murmur. JVP not raised. No ankle or sacral oedema.
  • Respiratory: normal expansion, resonant, vesicular breath sounds, no wheeze or crackles.
  • Abdomen: obese, soft, non-tender, no hepatomegaly.
  • Reflexes: normal, with normal relaxation.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as the junior doctor, confirms Martha's name and date of birth, explains the purpose of the consultation and gains consent for the history and examination.
Opens with an open question, acknowledges how the tiredness is affecting her work and mood, uses plain language and summarises back to her.
History
Characterises the tiredness:

Asks whether it is sleepiness (dozing off) or lack of energy, and finds it is sleepiness.
kids.d: Martha only says 'sleepy' if the candidate asks directly whether it is sleepiness, dozing or falling asleep, as opposed to lack of energy.

kids.x: Severity and pattern: 8/10, throughout the day, worse after a long day at work.
Impact: errors at work, poor concentration and memory, no energy to exercise, low mood.

Asks about snoring and witnessed pauses in breathing or gasping: chronic heavy snorer by her partner's report; partner a heavy sleeper who has not observed pauses.
Sleep hygiene: alcohol before bed, caffeine, sleeping tablets or sedatives.

check.x: Asks about sleepiness while driving: drowsy on the drive home after long days, no crashes or near misses.
check.d: Only given if the candidate asks about driving.

check.x: Uses cluster questions to screen at least 5 differentials:
check.d: Source marking: full credit for cluster questions covering at least 5 differentials together with the sleep hygiene questions; part credit for 3 or 4.

kids.x: Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin or hair (only a few kilos of weight gain).
Perimenopause: menstrual pattern, hot flushes, night sweats (periods regular, not menopausal).
Iron deficiency anaemia: heavy periods, gastrointestinal bleeding, breathlessness, palpitations (none).
Malignancy: weight loss, night sweats, fevers, lumps (none).
Heart failure and COPD: breathlessness, orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling; chronic cough, sputum, wheeze (none).
Depression: mood, loss of interest, and asks about thoughts of self-harm or suicide (low mood linked to sleepiness, interests intact, no self-harm thoughts).

check.x: Past medical history: hypertension for 5 years, type 2 diabetes for 10 years; not menopausal.
Medications (perindopril 5 mg daily, metformin 500 mg daily), over-the-counter medicines and supplements (none), and allergies (none known).
Family history: parents alive and well, no siblings.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Smoking quantified: 10 cigarettes a day for 20 years (10 pack-years).
Alcohol quantified: a glass or two of wine before bed most nights.
Work (scientist, not doing well), diet (could be better), exercise (none), lives with partner.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause and hopes it is not something bad.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs, noting BP 148/92 mmHg and SpO2 96% on room air.
Measures weight, height and BMI (36.0), waist circumference (112 cm) and neck circumference (42 cm).
check.d: Weight and BMI are critical; waist and neck circumference are needed for full marks.

check.x: Examines the upper airway: jaw position, nasal patency, and the oropharynx (crowded, Mallampati III, large tongue, low-lying soft palate, small tonsils).
Looks for signs of anaemia and hypothyroidism: conjunctival and palmar pallor, goitre, reflexes (all normal).
Examines the heart and lungs for heart failure, COPD or right heart strain: heart sounds, JVP, oedema, chest auscultation (all normal).
Interpretation
Questionnaires: ESS 15 (moderate excessive daytime sleepiness), STOP-Bang 5/8 and OSA50 6/10 (both high risk), giving a high probability of moderate to severe OSA.
Bloods: normal haemoglobin, iron studies and TSH, so anaemia, iron deficiency and hypothyroidism are unlikely causes.
Bloods: HbA1c 63 mmol/mol (7.9%) is above target and rising; ALT and GGT mildly raised (alcohol or fatty liver); renal function normal.

States the most likely diagnosis is obstructive sleep apnoea, justified by daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, heavy snoring, obesity with a large neck and crowded oropharynx, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, evening alcohol and the questionnaire scores.
Gives at least 4 differentials, each with a reason: hypothyroidism, perimenopause (age), iron deficiency anaemia, depression, malignancy, heart failure or COPD (smoker).
check.d: Source marking: half a mark for each differential with a reason, up to 4. A reason may be for or against (for example perimenopause because of her age; against: regular periods, no flushes).

check.x: States that the diagnosis and severity are confirmed by a sleep study (polysomnography, gold standard) using the apnoea-hypopnoea index: mild 5 to 14, moderate 15 to 30, severe above 30 events an hour.
Management
Arranges a sleep study: refers to a sleep specialist for polysomnography, or requests a home sleep study directly given her high-risk screening scores, with sleep physician involvement.

Explains the higher risk of motor vehicle crashes with untreated OSA, advises her not to drive when drowsy and to avoid driving after long days or whenever she feels sleepy until assessed and treated; explains she must notify the licensing authority if OSA with daytime sleepiness is confirmed (Austroads); expedites the sleep study because of drowsy driving.
check.d: Source marking stresses education about the higher risk of motor vehicle accidents.

check.x: Lifestyle measures:

kids.x: Weight loss, a healthy diet and regular moderate exercise.
Reduce alcohol, especially avoiding drinking before bed.
Stop smoking, with support (Quitline, pharmacotherapy).
Sleep hygiene and positional change (sleeping on her side).

check.x: Outlines treatment once OSA is confirmed: CPAP as first line for moderate to severe OSA; a mandibular advancement splint as an alternative (mild to moderate OSA or CPAP intolerance); surgery such as uvulopalatopharyngoplasty in selected cases.
check.d: CPAP as first line for moderate to severe OSA is the critical element.

check.x: Addresses her comorbidities: BP above target, HbA1c above target (diabetes review, metformin titration), and follow-up of the liver tests with alcohol reduction.

Explains the diagnosis to Martha in plain words (her throat relaxes and narrows during sleep, so her breathing is interrupted and her sleep broken), answers her worry that it is something bad, and checks her understanding.
Safety netting

Gives red flags in plain words with what to do: if she nods off or nearly does while driving, stop driving and see the GP; chest pain or severe breathlessness, call 000; new breathlessness or ankle swelling, see the GP soon; worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm, see the GP urgently or call Lifeline 13 11 14 (000 in an emergency).
check.d: Credit at least three red flags, each with the right action.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review with the sleep study result, plus review of her mood, blood pressure, diabetes and progress with smoking, alcohol and weight.

part2.lead: After your first consultation Martha had blood tests at the collection centre and completed sleep screening questionnaires with the practice nurse. She has come back a week later. Here are her questionnaire results and her blood results.
part2.patient: During the explanation (Q4), if not already covered, Martha asks only: 'Can I still drive to work?' She is relieved to have an explanation and uneasy about the driving advice, but accepts it if the candidate explains why.

handover.label: Sleep screening questionnaires
handover.result:
Completed with the practice nurse. Martha, 48. Weight 98 kg, height 165 cm (BMI 36.0), waist 112 cm, neck 42 cm.

Epworth Sleepiness Scale (chance of dozing, 0 = never to 3 = high chance):

  • Sitting and reading: 1
  • Watching TV: 3
  • Sitting inactive in a public place: 2
  • Passenger in a car for an hour without a break: 3
  • Lying down to rest in the afternoon: 3
  • Sitting and talking to someone: 0
  • Sitting quietly after lunch without alcohol: 2
  • In a car, while stopped for a few minutes in traffic: 1

Total: 15/24 (0 to 10 normal; 11 to 12 mild, 13 to 15 moderate, 16 to 24 severe excessive daytime sleepiness).

STOP-Bang: Snoring loudly, yes; Tired during the day, yes; Observed stopping breathing, no (partner a heavy sleeper); Pressure (treated hypertension), yes; BMI over 35, yes; Age over 50, no; Neck over 40 cm, yes; male Gender, no. Total: 5/8 (0 to 2 low, 3 to 4 intermediate, 5 to 8 high risk of OSA).

OSA50: Obesity (waist over 88 cm, women) 3; Snoring bothering others 3; witnessed Apnoeas 0; age 50 or over 0. Total: 6/10 (5 or more: high risk of OSA).
handover.model:
Read: ESS 15 is moderate excessive daytime sleepiness. She scores 1 for dozing when stopped in traffic. STOP-Bang 5/8 and OSA50 6/10 are both in the high-risk range.

For Martha: objective, significant daytime sleepiness and a high probability of moderate to severe OSA, driven by heavy snoring, obesity with a large neck and waist, and hypertension. No one has witnessed apnoeas, but her partner is a heavy sleeper, so this does not lower the risk. Questionnaires screen; they do not diagnose or grade OSA.

What it changes: she needs a diagnostic sleep study. Her scores meet the MBS item 12250 criteria for a GP to request an unattended home sleep study directly (ESS 8 or more, plus STOP-Bang 4 or more, OSA50 5 or more, or a high-risk Berlin questionnaire); otherwise refer to a sleep physician. Dozing in the car makes driving advice urgent.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 08:15, fasting. No haemolysis. Free T4 not performed because TSH is within the reference range.
handover.model:
Read: FBC normal (Hb 146, MCV 89). Iron studies normal (ferritin 85, saturation 26%). TSH 1.8, normal. Electrolytes and renal function normal (eGFR above 90). ALT 46 and GGT 62 mildly raised; bilirubin, ALP and albumin normal. HbA1c 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), up from 56 (7.3%) 6 months ago.

For Martha: anaemia, iron deficiency and hypothyroidism are excluded as causes of her sleepiness. The raised GGT and ALT fit her nightly alcohol and probable fatty liver with central obesity. Her diabetes control is above the usual target of 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) and worsening. Untreated OSA, weight, inactivity and alcohol all contribute.

What it changes: it supports OSA as the leading diagnosis. She needs a diabetes review (metformin is at a low dose and can be titrated; renal function allows this), alcohol reduction and repeat LFTs. These results do not need urgent action.

expect:
• Identify: self, junior doctor. Martha, 48, scientist.
  • Situation: several months of worsening daytime sleepiness; probable obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • Background: unrefreshing sleep, night waking, chronic heavy snoring, errors at work, low mood, drowsy driving home. Hypertension and T2DM on perindopril and metformin. 10 pack-years, 1 to 2 glasses of wine before bed most nights.
  • Assessment: BMI 36, neck 42 cm, waist 112 cm, crowded oropharynx, BP 148/92. ESS 15 (moderate sleepiness), STOP-Bang 5, OSA50 6: high risk. Hb, iron studies and TSH normal. HbA1c 63 and rising. ALT and GGT mildly raised.
  • Recommendation: sleep study (home study or sleep physician referral), driving advice, lifestyle measures, diabetes and BP review.

Most likely: obstructive sleep apnoea. For it: sleepiness rather than fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, heavy snoring, poor concentration, obesity, large neck, crowded oropharynx, hypertension, T2DM, smoking, evening alcohol, high-risk scores.

  • Hypothyroidism: tiredness and weight gain. Against: no other features, TSH normal.
  • Perimenopause: her age. Against: regular periods, no flushes or sweats.
  • Iron deficiency anaemia: against: normal Hb and iron studies.
  • Major depression: low mood. Against: secondary to sleepiness, interests intact.
  • Malignancy: age and smoking. Against: no weight loss or sweats.

Also accept heart failure or COPD (smoker; against: no breathlessness, cough or signs).

1. Confirm: sleep study, polysomnography (AHI: mild 5 to 14, moderate 15 to 30, severe above 30). High-risk scores allow a GP-requested home study, or refer to a sleep physician. Expedite the sleep study because of drowsy driving.
  2. Driving: higher crash risk; do not drive when drowsy, and avoid driving after long days or whenever sleepy until assessed and treated; must notify the licensing authority if OSA with daytime sleepiness is confirmed (Austroads).
  3. Lifestyle: weight loss, healthy diet, regular moderate exercise; reduce alcohol, none before bed; stop smoking (Quitline, pharmacotherapy); sleep hygiene; side sleeping.
  4. Once confirmed: CPAP first line for moderate to severe OSA; mandibular advancement splint; surgery (e.g. uvulopalatopharyngoplasty) in selected cases.
  5. Comorbidities: BP and diabetes review (titrate metformin), repeat LFTs, mood review.

• Explanation: her throat muscles relax and the airway narrows or closes during sleep, interrupting her breathing and breaking up her sleep, so she wakes unrefreshed and sleepy. Common, treatable, not cancer. Checks understanding.
  • Driving: sleepiness raises the crash risk. Do not drive when drowsy; avoid driving after long days or whenever she feels sleepy until assessed and treated. If OSA with daytime sleepiness is confirmed she must tell the licensing authority. The sleep study will be expedited.
  • Red flags: nodding off or near miss while driving, stop driving and see the GP; chest pain or severe breathlessness, call 000; new breathlessness or ankle swelling, see the GP soon; worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm, see the GP urgently or call Lifeline 13 11 14 (000 in an emergency).
  • Follow-up: GP review with the sleep study result; review mood, BP, diabetes, smoking, alcohol and weight.

guide:
Part 1: give the answers in the patient script only when asked. Martha says the tiredness is "sleepiness" only if the candidate asks whether it is sleepiness or lack of energy. Give the driving history only if driving is asked about. Item 8 follows the source marking: full credit for cluster questions covering at least five differentials together with the sleep hygiene questions, and part credit for three or four. Give examination findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. The source has no examination. The findings added here (obesity, large neck and waist, crowded oropharynx, raised BP) follow its teaching notes, and the driving history was added to support its emphasis on crash risk.

Part 2 is set a week later. Hand over both results together and ask the four questions in order. During the explanation (question 4), Martha asks about driving to work if it has not already been covered. Question 2 is the source's "top 4 differentials" task: credit item 25 for any four differentials, each with a reason. Questions 3 and 4 carry the source's management marks. Credit CPAP, splint and surgery (item 31) in either answer.

A high-performing candidate separates sleepiness from fatigue early and takes a sleep history that finds the snoring, alcohol before bed and drowsy driving. They screen at least five differentials in clusters, including mood and self-harm, and measure BMI, neck and waist and look at the oropharynx. In Part 2 they read the scores as high risk, use the bloods to exclude anaemia and hypothyroidism, and arrange a sleep study. They give clear driving advice and lifestyle measures and name CPAP as first line for moderate to severe OSA.

A borderline candidate takes a generic fatigue history without a sleep history or snoring question, misses the driving risk, diagnoses depression or menopause, or starts CPAP without a sleep study.
explain:
Diagnosis: obstructive sleep apnoea

Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is the commonest sleep-related breathing disorder. The upper airway repeatedly narrows or closes during sleep, causing episodes of reduced (hypopnoea) or absent (apnoea) airflow, arousals and broken sleep. Martha has the cardinal features: daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep despite 7 hours in bed, and a partner who reports loud, chronic snoring. Poor concentration, poor memory, errors at work and low mood are common consequences. Her risk factors are obesity (BMI 36) with a large neck and waist, a crowded oropharynx, smoking, alcohol before bed (which relaxes the upper airway muscles), hypertension and type 2 diabetes.

Sleepiness or fatigue?

Clarify this early. Sleepiness is a tendency to doze off when inactive, which points to a sleep disorder such as OSA. Fatigue is a lack of energy without falling asleep, as seen in anaemia, hypothyroidism, depression, chronic disease and malignancy. Patients use "tired" for both, so ask directly.

The history and examination

  • Sleep history: bedtime, hours of sleep, night waking, how refreshed they feel, snoring, witnessed apnoeas, gasping or choking, morning headaches or dry mouth, alcohol, caffeine and sedatives, shift work.
  • Driving: always ask about sleepiness at the wheel, near misses and crashes.
  • Cluster questions for the differentials: thyroid, menopause, anaemia and bleeding, malignancy (weight loss, sweats), heart failure and COPD, and mood, including self-harm.
  • Examination: BMI, neck and waist circumference, the jaw, nose and oropharynx (Mallampati class, tonsils), blood pressure, and signs of anaemia, hypothyroidism, heart failure and right heart strain.

Screening questionnaires

  • Epworth Sleepiness Scale: measures daytime sleepiness, not OSA. Above 10 is excessive sleepiness; Martha's 15 is moderate.
  • STOP-Bang (5 or more is high risk) and OSA50 (5 or more is high risk): estimate the probability of OSA.

Her scores meet the MBS item 12250 criteria for a GP to request an unattended home sleep study directly (ESS 8 or more, plus STOP-Bang 4 or more, OSA50 5 or more, or a high-risk Berlin questionnaire); otherwise refer to a sleep physician.

The other results

A normal blood count, iron studies and TSH exclude anaemia, iron deficiency and hypothyroidism. Her HbA1c of 63 mmol/mol is above target and rising. Mildly raised ALT and GGT fit alcohol and fatty liver. Both are worth acting on, and both share risk factors with OSA.

The differentials

  • Hypothyroidism: excluded by a normal TSH.
  • Perimenopause: considered because of her age, but her periods are regular with no vasomotor symptoms.
  • Iron deficiency anaemia: excluded by normal Hb and iron studies.
  • Major depression: her low mood follows the sleepiness and her interests are intact. Screen for it and reassess once OSA is treated.
  • Malignancy: no weight loss, sweats or lumps.
  • Heart failure and COPD: no breathlessness, orthopnoea, oedema, cough or wheeze. Both also raise the risk of OSA.

Confirming the diagnosis

Polysomnography is the gold standard. It measures the apnoea-hypopnoea index (AHI), the number of events per hour of sleep:

  • mild: 5 to 14
  • moderate: 15 to 30
  • severe: above 30

Management (eTG Respiratory)

  • Education: untreated OSA brings a higher risk of motor vehicle crashes, as well as hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
  • Lifestyle:
    • weight loss, a healthy diet and regular moderate exercise;
    • reduce alcohol and avoid it before bed; avoid sedatives;
    • stop smoking, with Quitline (13 7848) and pharmacotherapy;
    • sleep hygiene;
    • positional therapy (side sleeping), when apnoeas are worse lying on the back.
  • CPAP: first line for moderate to severe OSA, started and titrated with a sleep service.
  • Mandibular advancement splint: fitted by a dentist, for mild to moderate OSA or when CPAP is not tolerated.
  • Surgery: for example uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, in selected patients.
  • Comorbidities: blood pressure and diabetes review, liver follow-up and mood review.

Driving

Under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive (2022), a private driver with established sleep apnoea (AHI 5 or more) and excessive daytime sleepiness, or a crash caused by sleepiness, does not meet the standard for an unconditional licence. The licensing authority may grant a conditional licence on the treating doctor's report that she uses treatment and it works (sleep specialist opinion is needed for commercial drivers). Once diagnosed, she must tell the licensing authority. Because Martha already feels drowsy at the wheel, advise her not to drive when drowsy and to avoid driving after long days or whenever she feels sleepy until assessed and treated, and expedite her sleep study.

Safety netting

  • Driving: stop driving and see the GP if she nods off or has a near miss at the wheel.
  • Call 000: chest pain or severe breathlessness.
  • See the GP soon: new breathlessness or ankle swelling.
  • Mood: if her mood worsens or she has thoughts of self-harm, see the GP urgently or call Lifeline (13 11 14), or 000 in an emergency.
  • Follow-up: review with the sleep study result, and continued review of BP, diabetes, weight, alcohol and smoking.
points: Separate sleepiness (dozing off) from fatigue (lack of energy) early. Sleepiness points to a sleep disorder such as OSA.
In any tired patient, take a sleep history: hours, unrefreshing sleep, snoring, witnessed apnoeas, alcohol and sedatives, and sleepiness while driving.
Screen the differentials with cluster questions (thyroid, menopause, anaemia, malignancy, heart failure, COPD, depression including self-harm), and confirm with FBC, iron studies and TSH.
ESS measures sleepiness; STOP-Bang and OSA50 estimate the risk of OSA. Polysomnography confirms the diagnosis and grades it by AHI: mild 5 to 14, moderate 15 to 30, severe above 30.
CPAP is first line for moderate to severe OSA, with weight loss, less alcohol, stopping smoking and side sleeping for everyone; splints and surgery are alternatives.
Untreated OSA increases the crash risk: advise no driving when drowsy, and explain licence obligations under Austroads.
